content:
[paulus_figure name="isaiah-scroll"]The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, second century BCE, Israel Museum, Jerusalem, at Isaiah 53: the Hebrew scriptures in the form they had long before Paul quoted them.[/paulus_figure]

Paul also played a chief part in shaping the New Testament through the distortion of the Jewish scriptures (the Tanakh) in support of a theology that departed from the teaching of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām). Cunningly, his followers or he himself twisted direct quotations from the Old Testament to attract Gentiles and cut the teaching of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam from its Jewish roots.

One chief example is the quotation of Jeremiah 31:31–34 in the Epistle to the Hebrews, whose authorship is attributed to Paul although textual critics dispute it.1 The theology of the letter reflects Paul's agenda of replacing the covenant of the Torah with a new covenant through Jesus Christ.2 The original text of Jeremiah (hinnēh yāmîm bāʾîm, הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים, "Behold, the days are coming") foretold a new covenant with Israel and Judah, promising the Torah written on the heart and the forgiveness of sins.3

The Epistle to the Hebrews altered the meaning of the text. The phrase "though I was their husband" (Jeremiah 31:32, bāʿaltî bām, בָּעַלְתִּי בָם) is replaced by "and so I showed no concern for them" (kai egō ēmelēsa autōn, καὶ ἐγὼ ἠμέλησα αὐτῶν) following the Septuagint (LXX).

The Jeremiah text, which joins knowledge of God to unconditional forgiveness, is separated from its context in Hebrews by foregrounding forgiveness through the doctrine of redemption on the cross.4 The choice portrays God as having rejected Israel and as sanctioning the abolition of the law that ʿĪsā ibn Maryam had confirmed.5

31Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, 32not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD.6

8μεμφόμενος γὰρ αὐτοὺς λέγει· Ἰδοὺ ἡμέραι ἔρχονται, λέγει κύριος, καὶ συντελέσω ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰούδα διαθήκην καινήν, 9οὐ κατὰ τὴν διαθήκην ἣν ἐποίησα τοῖς πατράσιν αὐτῶν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπιλαβομένου μου τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῶν ἐξαγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅτι αὐτοὶ οὐκ ἐνέμειναν ἐν τῇ διαθήκῃ μου, κἀγὼ ἠμέλησα αὐτῶν, λέγει κύριος.

8For he finds fault with them when he says: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, 9not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.7

The letter then draws its conclusion from the prophecy: "In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away."8 Jeremiah says the reverse.

[paulus_figure name="hebrew-letters-old-book-4033818"]Hebrew letters in a printed text. Paul quotes the Scriptures, often from the Greek translation, and bends them to his own argument.[/paulus_figure]

The promise the letter has just quoted reads "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts": the new covenant is the law of Mūsā written on the heart, and Jeremiah gives no sign that it will vanish.9 The letter quotes the verse in full and draws from it the one conclusion it cannot bear.

The pattern recurs, mutatis mutandis, in Galatians, where Paul twists a quotation from Genesis 12:7 (lezarʿăkā, לְזַרְעֲךָ, "to your offspring"), turning "offspring" (zeraʿ, זֶרַע, a singular noun with collective meaning) into a word referring to Jesus (sperma, σπέρμα, "offspring," singular) to support his Christology.10 The real text of Genesis refers to all the descendants of Ibrāhīm, but Paul changed it to justify Jesus as the fulfiller of the promise.

16τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ ἐρρέθησαν αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ· οὐ λέγει· Καὶ τοῖς σπέρμασιν, ὡς ἐπὶ πολλῶν, ἀλλʼ ὡς ἐφʼ ἑνός· Καὶ τῷ σπέρματί σου, ὅς ἐστιν Χριστός.

16Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, "And to offsprings," referring to many, but referring to one, "And to your offspring," who is Christ.11

The letter to the Ephesians, written in Paul's name, quotes Psalm 68:18 (lāqaḥtā mattānôt, לָקַחְתָּ מַתָּנוֹת, "receiving gifts among men") but changes "received" (lāqaḥtā) to "gave" (edōken, ἔδωκεν), portraying Jesus as bestowing spiritual gifts.12 The Psalm refers to God's victory and says nothing of the Messiah; the writer altered the verse to support the doctrine of Paul's school.

In 1 Corinthians Paul gives Isaiah 64:4 (lōʾ rāʾătāh ʿayin, לֹא רָאֲתָה עַיִן, "no eye has seen") in paraphrase and ties divine wisdom to Jesus, although the Isaiah text refers to God's future action for Israel. The loose paraphrase (ha kategrapsen, ἃ κατεγράψεν, "as it is written") departs from the original context and serves only to reinforce Paul's narrative.13

[paulus_figure name="ancient-scroll-fragment-museum-11455009"]An ancient scroll in a dimly lit museum case. Paul writes “as it is written” over a chain of verses drawn from several psalms and Isaiah (Romans 3:10–18).[/paulus_figure]

One more striking example is in Romans, where Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30:11–14 (kî-qārôb ʾēleykā haddābār, כִּי־קָרוֹב אֵלֶיךָ הַדָּבָר, "the word is very near you"), which affirms that God's commandment is within reach without searching heaven or crossing the sea. Paul changes the meaning by tying it to righteousness through faith in Jesus (peri dikaiosynēs tēs ek pisteōs, περὶ δικαιοσύνης τῆς ἐκ πίστεως, "the righteousness based on faith") and makes Jesus the fulfiller of the word. That replaces the direct accessibility of the Torah with a reading centered on Jesus.14

11For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off. 12It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' 13Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, 'Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' 14But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.15

6ἡ δὲ ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοσύνη οὕτως λέγει· Μὴ εἴπῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου· Τίς ἀναβήσεται εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν; τοῦτʼ ἔστιν Χριστὸν καταγαγεῖν· 7ἤ· Τίς καταβήσεται εἰς τὴν ἄβυσσον; τοῦτʼ ἔστιν Χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναγαγεῖν. 8ἀλλὰ τί λέγει; Ἐγγύς σου τὸ ῥῆμά ἐστιν, ἐν τῷ στόματί σου καὶ ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου, τοῦτʼ ἔστιν τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως ὃ κηρύσσομεν.

6But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down) 7"or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). 8But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);16

Paul's influence on the New Testament cannot be denied. Through his letters he introduced the doctrines that form the basis of Christian teaching today, and he also created a false mechanism of interpretation that allowed revelation to be distorted systematically and inherited by Christian institutions to this day. From justification by faith to freedom from the law, Paul's teaching continues to shape the growth and spread of Christianity.

The changes Paul made damage the New Testament theologically. Where his teachings came from was the question of the fourth count. What they became is the question of the last: a religion that bears the name of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam and follows the teaching of Paul.
